summary: Documents methods applications use to set up direct peer-to-peer communication through Network Address Translators. It is mostly descriptive, with advisory security recommendations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Home routers hide computers behind one address, which blocks direct contact. This lists the tricks programs use to still talk straight to each other.

questions: how do peers connect through nat
subtitle: How peer-to-peer programs get through home routers that only expect outgoing connections.

tldr.problem: NAT devices were built for client/server traffic, so hosts behind them have no permanently visible public port that a peer can connect to. That breaks peer-to-peer applications such as teleconferencing and multiplayer gaming.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents the techniques applications already use without changing the NAT: relaying through a rendezvous server, connection reversal, UDP and TCP hole punching, and port number prediction.
tldr.outcome: Hole punching is the most efficient method but only works through NATs that use Endpoint-Independent Mapping, so applications should be ready to fall back to relaying. The memo is descriptive and not an endorsement.

today: RFC 5128 is an Informational memo from March 2008 and, per its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the techniques known at that time and does not endorse them.

sections.title: Why NATs Break Peer-to-Peer
sections.content:
Deployed NAT devices are designed around the client/server model: anonymous clients inside a private network open connections to public servers. That works for web browsers, which only make outgoing connections. In the peer-to-peer model, hosts that would normally be clients also accept sessions from other peers, and both sides may sit behind different NATs with no permanent public address.

A typical design has every host contact a publicly addressable rendezvous server to register and find peers, then connect directly. The RFC notes that these problems are likely to persist even in an IPv6 world, since firewalls filter in a similar way to NATs.

The memo describes techniques that work without altering the NAT devices. Techniques that signal explicitly to the NAT (such as UPnP or NAT-PMP) are out of scope, and so are timeouts and keepalives for a running session. It covers TCP and UDP applications only.
sections.eli5: Most home networks only let your computer call out, not get called. Games and video chats need two computers to call each other, so they need special tricks.

sections.title: Mapping, Filtering and Hairpinning
sections.content:
The RFC borrows its vocabulary from RFC 4787 instead of the older "Full Cone" and "Symmetric" names, which it says caused much confusion. An endpoint is an (IP address, port) pair. Endpoint mapping is the public endpoint a NAT assigns to translate a private one.

  • Endpoint-Independent Mapping: the NAT reuses the same port mapping for packets from one internal address and port to any external destination.
  • Endpoint-Dependent Mapping: the mapping is reused only for the same external address, or the same external address and port.
  • Filtering decides which incoming packets are let in. Endpoint-Independent Filtering accepts them from any external endpoint. Endpoint-Dependent Filtering requires the internal host to have sent to that address (or address and port) first.

A NAT with Endpoint-Independent Mapping is called an EIM-NAT, and it can have any filtering behavior. Hairpinning is when a NAT loops traffic from one internal host to another internal host via its public address. The RFC notes that not all deployed NATs support it.
sections.eli5: A NAT keeps a list of who inside talked to whom outside. Some NATs use the same door number for every conversation, which helps peers find you. Others pick a new door each time, which makes it hard.

sections.title: Relaying and Connection Reversal
sections.content:
Relaying is the most reliable but least efficient method. Both clients keep their outgoing connections to a rendezvous server S, and S forwards messages between them. It always works as long as both clients can reach S, and the NATs do not need to be EIM-NAT. The cost is server processing power and network bandwidth, and likely extra latency. The TURN protocol defines a way to do application-agnostic packet relay.

Connection reversal works only when exactly one peer is behind a NAT. If public client B cannot connect in, it asks A, through server S, to open the connection to B instead. NAT A allows it because it is an outgoing connection. When both peers are behind NATs it fails, so applications often fall back to relaying.
sections.eli5: Relaying is passing notes through a friend in the middle. Connection reversal is when you cannot call your friend, so you ask them to call you instead.

sections.title: Hole Punching and Port Prediction
sections.content:
UDP hole punching relies on EIM-NATs. Both clients first talk to server S, so S learns each one's public endpoint and passes it on. Then A starts sending UDP messages to B's public endpoint while B does the same to A's. Each NAT sees an outgoing message and opens a mapping, so the other side's packets are now accepted. S ends up as an "introduction" server only. The application does not need to detect the NAT type, and it works through several levels of NAT.

If both clients are behind the same NAT, sending to public endpoints depends on hairpinning. To avoid that, peers also exchange their own private endpoints and use whichever address works first. Those packets must be authenticated, because messages sent to a private address may reach an unrelated host.

TCP hole punching uses "Simultaneous TCP Open": both sides send SYN at the same time. It is not implemented correctly on many systems, and a SYN arriving too early can be dropped or answered with a RST, which can break the attempt.

Port number prediction (the "N+1" technique) tries to work through some NATs with Endpoint-Dependent Mapping by guessing the next port the NAT will assign. The RFC calls it fragile: it fails if the NAT does not assign ports sequentially, if the port is already in use, or if another client behind the NAT grabs the port. The TCP variant is even more timing-sensitive.
sections.eli5: Both friends knock on each other's door at the same moment. Each door sees its own owner knocked first, so it opens when the reply comes. Guessing the next door number can work, but only if nobody else sneaks in first.

sections.title: Measured Results and Observations
sections.content:
The RFC cites test results from a NAT check program across commercial devices. UDP hole punching worked on more than 80% of the NATs tested, TCP hole punching on just over 60%, and fewer than 25% passed the hairpinning tests. A later study found that more sophisticated techniques let up to 88% of deployed NATs support TCP hole punching. Another source in the text reports that more than 50% of NAT devices support Endpoint-Independent Mapping and do not send RSTs or ICMP errors to unsolicited SYNs.

Its summary: hole punching is the most efficient method between two NATed hosts, but only through an EIM-NAT, and a substantial fraction of NATs use Endpoint-Dependent Mapping. Applications should be ready to fall back to relaying. Registering private endpoints as well as public ones with the rendezvous server helps peers on the same NAT, and hairpinning support matters most for large first-level NATs in multi-level setups. The text also mentions Teredo and ICE as protocols built on these ideas.
sections.eli5: Most home routers let the trick work, but not all. So smart programs keep a backup plan of passing messages through a middle server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says it creates no new security issues but lists risks that applications could introduce. All four come back to authentication.

  • Connection hijacking: hole-punching probes can reach unintended hosts, for example when two private networks use the same default address range. Applications must authenticate and should treat any reported address as suspect until authenticated two-way communication exists.
  • Denial of service: a host can register someone else's address with the rendezvous server. Applications and servers must avoid costly work and must size- and rate-limit traffic to unverified addresses.
  • Man-in-the-middle: any device on the path can pretend to be a NAT and alter the source address in a registration. The only defense is authenticating and encrypting application content.
  • EIM-NAT impact: Endpoint-Independent Mapping with Endpoint-Dependent Filtering is no more promiscuous than Endpoint-Dependent Mapping, though it makes traffic more predictable.
sections.eli5: Because you are knocking on doors you are not sure about, you must check who answers. Otherwise you might talk to the wrong person.
